intro: Welcome! At work and when you travel you'll meet British, American and Australian speakers, but also Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian ones, and many people who, like you, speak English as an extra language. In this lesson you learn the words and the sounds that mark each variety, and how to be clearly understood when English is the language you share.
teachingNotes: Recap and build: b2-listening-extended taught UK/US/AU differences as TENDENCIES (r after a vowel said in the US but mostly not in England/Australia; US t between vowels as a soft d: water → 'wader'; Australian 'ay' close to 'ai': day ≈ 'die'; US 'o' in hot ≈ 'haht'). Recap that in one line, don't re-teach it. Go further: the full map of r after a vowel, plus Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian English, and English as a lingua franca (ELF). Present every variety as equally valid (Indian English is not 'broken British English'); Indonesian English is a variety too. Features are tendencies ('often', 'tends to', 'many speakers'), clues for listening, never labels for people.

AUDIO LIMIT: every recording in the app is ONE text-to-speech voice with ONE accent. Never claim a recording shows an accent. `listen` questions only test what comes from the WORDS (vocabulary and expressions typical of a variety); pronunciation features are taught and tested in text. For real accents, point to the resources (The New Travel's video with speakers from many countries).

Vocabulary by variety (for understanding, not for the learner to copy): UK lift / US elevator; UK flat / US apartment; UK on holiday / US on vacation; UK ground floor = the street level (Indonesian lantai 1), UK first floor = one level up (lantai 2; US second floor). Australia: arvo = afternoon, brekkie = breakfast, No worries = it's fine / you're welcome. India: prepone = move to an earlier time (opposite of postpone), revert = reply (elsewhere revert = go back to an earlier state), do the needful = do what is necessary, lakh = 100,000, crore = 10 million, out of station = away from town. Singapore: Standard Singapore English (work, school, news) vs Singlish (informal; words from Malay, Hokkien and others): Can or not? = is it possible? / can you? (Can = yes, Cannot = no), particles lah (emphasis, reassurance), leh (softer, persuading or unsure), lor (accepting: that's how it is), chope = reserve a seat. Nigeria: I'm coming = I'll be right back (said when leaving for a moment), go-slow = traffic jam, well done = a greeting to someone at work.

Pronunciation features (text only, as tendencies). r after a vowel (car, card, four, water): usually SAID in the US and Canada, Ireland, Scotland and much of India; usually NOT said in most of England, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Nigeria; non-r speakers often say it before a vowel (far away → 'faa-raway'). Rhythm: UK/US/AU are stress-timed (weak syllables squeezed into a short 'uh'); Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian English are often syllable-timed, like Indonesian (syllables of similar length, clearer vowels). India: t and d often said with the tongue tip curled back (retroflex); many speakers use one sound between v and w for both letters. Singapore: the final consonant is often very soft or dropped (stop → 'sto'), long and short vowels less different. Nigeria: less vowel reduction (full vowels in weak syllables: about → 'a-baut'). In all three, th often → t/d (think → 'tink'). Describe sounds with everyday spellings, no bare IPA.

ELF: English between people with different first languages (Japanese, Thai, German, Korean partners). Clear beats clever: avoid idioms (touch base, call it a day, hit the ground running, ballpark figure), slang and abbreviations (ASAP, EOD, OOO); one idea per sentence; slow down a little at key points; say key numbers digit by digit (one-five) and type them in the chat; spell names (S for Surabaya); write dates with the month as a word (03/04 = 3 April in Indonesia/UK but March 4 in the US); check understanding with a summary (Just to confirm, … / So, to sum up, …) rather than 'Do you understand?'; paraphrase (What I mean is … / Let me put it another way). Lingua Franca Core (Jennifer Jenkins), simply: consonants (th matters little), sounds at the start of words, long vs short vowels (ship/sheep, a trap for Indonesians) and stress on the key word matter more than a native accent.

Common errors to target: thinking non-native varieties are wrong; taking Nigerian 'I'm coming' literally; reading the UK 'first floor' as lantai 1; reading Indian 'revert' as 'go back'; thinking British speakers drop every r (they say it in red, very); thinking only Americans say the r; mixing up Singlish with Standard Singapore English; the Indonesian polite 'yes' (sungkan) without understanding, and asking 'Do you understand?'; using idioms, slang and abbreviations with international partners; spending energy on imitating a native accent instead of being clear. Limits: A0–B2 grammar only (no inversion, cleft sentences, subjunctive); the learner should understand Singlish and Nigerian expressions, not produce them; answers are short: accept the meaning, not exact words.

keyPoints.title: Understand other varieties: local words, context and tuning in
keyPoints.explanation: Many varieties have their own everyday words. UK lift / US elevator, and the UK first floor is one level above the ground floor. Australian arvo = afternoon. Indian English: prepone = move earlier, revert = reply, do the needful = do what is necessary, lakh = 100,000. Singlish: Can or not? = is it possible? Nigerian English: I'm coming = I'll be right back. With a new variety, give yourself a minute to tune in, follow the stressed key words and the context, and if a word is new, ask: it may be a local word, not your mistake.

examples.id: Sampai jumpa sore ini. (Australia: arvo = afternoon)

examples.en: The meeting has been preponed to 9 a.m.
examples.id: Rapatnya dimajukan ke jam 9 pagi. (India: prepone = memajukan jadwal)
Tunggu sebentar, saya segera kembali. (Nigeria: I'm coming = saya segera kembali)

id.title: Memahami ragam lain: kata lokal, konteks dan menyesuaikan telinga
id.explanation: Banyak ragam punya kata sehari-hari sendiri. UK lift / US elevator, dan first floor di Inggris adalah satu lantai di atas lantai dasar. Bahasa Australia arvo = sore/siang. Bahasa Inggris India: prepone = memajukan jadwal, revert = membalas, do the needful = lakukan apa yang diperlukan, lakh = 100.000. Singlish: Can or not? = bisa atau tidak? Bahasa Inggris Nigeria: I'm coming = saya segera kembali. Saat bertemu ragam baru, beri dirimu satu menit untuk menyesuaikan telinga, ikuti kata kunci yang ditekan dan konteksnya, dan kalau ada kata baru, tanyakan: mungkin itu kata lokal, bukan kesalahanmu.

keyPoints.title: Key sound features of each variety (tendencies)
keyPoints.explanation: r after a vowel (car, card): usually said in the US and Canada, Scotland, Ireland and much of India; usually not said in most of England, Australia, Singapore and Nigeria. Recap: US t between vowels sounds like a soft d (water → 'wader'); Australian day sounds close to 'die'. UK, US and Australian English are stress-timed (weak syllables squeezed into 'uh'); Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian English are often syllable-timed, like Indonesian. India: t and d with the tongue tip curled back, and often one sound for v and w. Singapore: the last consonant is often soft or dropped. Nigeria: full, clear vowels in weak syllables. In all three, think often sounds like 'tink'.

examples.id: sangat baik · India: v dan w sering satu bunyi yang sama

id.title: Ciri bunyi utama tiap ragam (kecenderungan)
id.explanation: r setelah vokal (car, card): biasanya dibaca di Amerika dan Kanada, Skotlandia, Irlandia dan sebagian besar India; biasanya tidak dibaca di sebagian besar Inggris, Australia, Singapura dan Nigeria. Ulangan: t Amerika di antara dua vokal terdengar seperti d yang lembut (water → 'wader'); day Australia terdengar mirip 'die'. Bahasa Inggris UK, US dan Australia berirama tekanan (stress-timed: suku kata lemah dipendekkan jadi 'eu'); bahasa Inggris India, Singapura dan Nigeria sering berirama suku kata (syllable-timed), seperti bahasa Indonesia. India: t dan d dengan ujung lidah melengkung ke belakang, dan v serta w sering satu bunyi. Singapura: konsonan terakhir sering lemah atau hilang. Nigeria: vokal penuh dan jelas di suku kata lemah. Di ketiganya, think sering terdengar 'tink'.

keyPoints.title: English as a lingua franca: clear beats clever
keyPoints.explanation: When English is the shared language between non-native speakers, being clear matters more than sounding native. Avoid idioms, slang and abbreviations (touch base, ASAP, EOD). Say key numbers digit by digit and type them in the chat, spell names, write the month as a word (03/04 means different dates in different countries). Check understanding with a summary (Just to confirm, … / So, to sum up, …), not 'Do you understand?'. Paraphrase when someone looks lost (What I mean is …). The Lingua Franca Core: clear consonants, long vs short vowels and stress on the key word matter more than a native accent.

examples.en: Just to confirm: the deadline is 3 April.

examples.id: Itu satu-lima: lima belas ribu unit.

examples.en: What I mean is, we need more time.
examples.id: Maksud saya, kami butuh waktu lebih.

id.title: Bahasa Inggris sebagai lingua franca: jelas lebih penting daripada keren
id.explanation: Saat bahasa Inggris menjadi bahasa bersama antar-penutur non-native, jelas lebih penting daripada terdengar seperti penutur asli. Hindari idiom, slang dan singkatan (touch base, ASAP, EOD). Ucapkan angka penting digit per digit dan ketik di chat, eja nama, tulis bulan dengan kata (03/04 berarti tanggal yang berbeda di negara yang berbeda). Cek pemahaman dengan ringkasan (Just to confirm, … / So, to sum up, …), bukan 'Do you understand?'. Ucapkan ulang dengan kata lain kalau lawan bicara tampak bingung (What I mean is …). Lingua Franca Core: konsonan yang jelas, vokal panjang vs pendek dan tekanan pada kata kunci lebih penting daripada aksen penutur asli.

guidedPractice.prompt: Pak Hasan is in the lobby of a London hotel, on the ground floor. The receptionist says his meeting room is on the first floor. How many floors does he need to go up? Write a number.
guidedPractice.hint: In the UK the ground floor is the street level; the first floor is the next one up.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your host in Brisbane says: 'Brekkie is at seven.' Which meal is that? One word.
guidedPractice.hint: Australians often shorten words: arvo = afternoon. This one is the first meal of the day.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your colleague in Singapore says: 'Meet you at the bus stop.' In Singapore English, which consonant at the end of 'stop' may be very soft or hard to hear? Write the letter.
guidedPractice.hint: Singapore English often softens or drops the LAST consonant of a word.

guidedPractice.prompt: On a call with partners from Japan and Germany, you want to ask: 'Can you give me a ballpark figure?' Replace the idiom 'a ballpark figure' with plain words.
expected: a rough idea of the cost
guidedPractice.hint: A ballpark figure is a number that is not exact, only about right.

independentPractice.prompt: Your colleague in Mumbai says the budget for the launch event is 'three lakh rupees'. Write the amount in digits.
Many Indian English speakers say t and d with the tip of the tongue curled back. What is this kind of sound called? One word.
A US colleague writes: 'Deadline: 03/04/2027.' In American date style, which month is the deadline? Write the month in English.
independentPractice.hint: In the US the month comes first; in Indonesia and the UK the day comes first.

assessment.prompt: You're on a video call with Chidi, a colleague in Lagos, Nigeria. He stands up and says this. Listen. What does he mean? Answer in English in a few words.
assessment.listen: Sorry, Bu Ani, the delivery man is at the gate. I'm coming.
acceptableAnswers: he'll be back in a minute
he will be back in a minute
he is leaving for a moment
assessment.rubric: Correct: he'll be right back (Nigerian English 'I'm coming' = I'm leaving for a moment and will return). The right idea in Indonesian (sebentar, dia segera kembali) = 70. 'he is going to the gate' alone = 50 (true, but misses that he'll come back). 'he is coming to Bu Ani / he is joining us' = 0 (the standard British/American meaning, wrong here). 'the delivery man is coming' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Wei Ling, a colleague in Singapore, sends you a voice message. Listen. What does she want to know? Answer in English in a few words.
assessment.listen: Hi Budi, Wei Ling here. The client wants the slides by three o'clock today. Can or not?
acceptableAnswers: if i can send the slides by three
whether i can send the slides by three
can i send the slides by three
can you send the slides by three
if i can send them by three
can you send them by three
if the slides can be ready by three
if i can finish the slides by three
if i can do it by three
can you do it by three
if budi can send the slides by three
assessment.rubric: Correct: whether Budi can send/finish the slides by three (Singlish 'Can or not?' = is it possible? / can you?). The right idea in Indonesian (bisa atau tidak) = 70. 'the client wants the slides' alone = 30 (the fact, not her question). 'she wants to know if the client can come' = 0. Any time other than three = 50 at most.

assessment.prompt: Mr Sharma, your manager in Bengaluru, ends an email: 'The auditors arrive on Monday. Kindly do the needful.' What does 'do the needful' mean? Answer in English in a few words.
acceptableAnswers: do what needs to be done
do what you need to do
assessment.rubric: Correct: do what is necessary (Indian English; here: prepare what the auditors need). The right idea in Indonesian (lakukan apa yang diperlukan) = 70. 'meet the auditors' alone = 50 (a possible part, too narrow). 'do nothing' / 'it's not needed' = 0. 'help the auditors' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Rina has two colleagues: Fiona from Glasgow, Scotland, and Mia from Sydney, Australia. Both say the word 'car'. Who is more likely to pronounce the r? Write the name.
assessment.rubric: Correct: Fiona (Scottish English usually says the r after a vowel; most Australian speakers don't). 'Mia' = 0. 'both' / 'neither' = 0. 'the one from Scotland' = 100.

assessment.prompt: Many speakers in Nigeria, India and Singapore give every syllable a similar length and a clear vowel, like Indonesian does. British and American English instead squeeze the weak syllables between the stressed ones. What is the first kind of rhythm called? Write the term.
assessment.rubric: Correct: syllable-timed. 'stress-timed' = 0 (that's the British and American rhythm). 'syllable stress' = 30 (close word, wrong idea). 'berirama suku kata' (Indonesian) = 70.

assessment.prompt: It's 6 p.m. and a long online meeting with partners from Thailand and Germany is going nowhere. You want to say 'Let's call it a day.' Say it in plain words, without the idiom. Write a short sentence.
acceptableAnswers: let's end the meeting for today
assessment.rubric: Correct: a plain sentence meaning 'let's stop (for today)'. Small grammar slips with the right meaning = 80. A sentence that keeps the idiom ('let's call it a day') = 0 (the task is to avoid it). Another idiom ('let's wrap it up') = 40 (right meaning, but still not plain). 'let's take a break' = 40 (a pause, not the end).

assessment.prompt: On a bad phone line, Somchai, a supplier in Bangkok, tells you the price per box. You can't tell if he said 'fifteen' or 'fifty'. Write one short question to check the number.
acceptableAnswers: did you say fifteen or fifty
is that one five or five zero
is it one five or five zero
did you say one five or five zero
could you say the number again
could you say the number digit by digit
could you write the number in the chat
can you type the number in the chat
assessment.rubric: Correct: a short question that checks the number: 'Is that fifteen or fifty?', 'One-five or five-zero?', or asking him to repeat, say it digit by digit or type it. Best answers name both options or ask for digits. 'Do you understand?' = 0 (it checks him, not the number). 'OK' / 'yes' = 0 (no check). A correct idea with small grammar slips = 80.

id.title: Banyak ragam bahasa Inggris, semuanya sah

blocks.text:
In B2 you learnt that British, American and Australian English differ in **tendencies**: the r in *car*, the soft d in *water*, the Australian *day*. Now we widen the map.

English is the first language of the UK, the US, Australia and a few other countries, but **far more people speak it as a second or extra language** than as a first. In **India**, **Singapore** and **Nigeria**, English is an official language, used every day in offices, universities, courts and the media. Each of these places has its own **variety** (ragam) of English, with its own words, sounds and rhythm.

Three ideas to keep:
- **All varieties are equally valid.** Indian English is not 'broken British English': it's Indian English. Your **Indonesian English** is a variety too.
- **Standard and local.** Most varieties have a standard form (news, reports, school) and a relaxed local form. In Singapore, **Standard Singapore English** is used at work and at school; **Singlish** is the informal, friendly version, with words from Malay, Hokkien (a Chinese language) and other languages. Many Singaporeans switch between the two.
- **Features are tendencies.** Not every Australian says 'die' for *day*, and not every Indian speaker uses Indian words. Use the features as clues for listening, not as labels for people.

**How to listen to a new variety:** give yourself a minute or two to **tune in** (menyesuaikan telinga): the first sentences are always the hardest. Hold on to the **stressed key words** and the **context**. If a word is new, it may be a **local word**, not your mistake: ask *'Sorry, what does … mean?'*

id.text:
Di B2 kamu belajar bahwa bahasa Inggris versi Inggris, Amerika dan Australia berbeda dalam **kecenderungan**: r di *car*, d lembut di *water*, *day* versi Australia. Sekarang petanya kita perluas.

Bahasa Inggris adalah bahasa pertama di Inggris, Amerika, Australia dan beberapa negara lain, tapi **jauh lebih banyak orang memakainya sebagai bahasa kedua atau tambahan** daripada sebagai bahasa pertama. Di **India**, **Singapura** dan **Nigeria**, bahasa Inggris adalah bahasa resmi, dipakai setiap hari di kantor, kampus, pengadilan dan media. Tiap tempat itu punya **ragam** (variety) bahasa Inggrisnya sendiri, dengan kata, bunyi dan iramanya sendiri.

Tiga hal yang perlu diingat:
- **Semua ragam sama sahnya.** Bahasa Inggris India bukan 'bahasa Inggris Inggris yang rusak': itu bahasa Inggris India. **Bahasa Inggris orang Indonesia** juga sebuah ragam.
- **Baku dan lokal.** Kebanyakan ragam punya bentuk baku (berita, laporan, sekolah) dan bentuk lokal yang santai. Di Singapura, **Standard Singapore English** dipakai di kantor dan sekolah; **Singlish** adalah versi santai dan akrabnya, dengan kata-kata dari bahasa Melayu, Hokkien (salah satu bahasa Tionghoa) dan bahasa lain. Banyak orang Singapura berganti-ganti di antara keduanya.
- **Ciri-ciri itu kecenderungan.** Tidak semua orang Australia mengucapkan *day* seperti 'die', dan tidak semua penutur India memakai kata-kata khas India. Pakai ciri-ciri ini sebagai petunjuk saat mendengarkan, bukan sebagai label untuk orang.

**Cara mendengarkan ragam baru:** beri dirimu satu-dua menit untuk **menyesuaikan telinga** (tune in): kalimat-kalimat pertama selalu yang paling sulit. Pegang **kata kunci yang ditekan** dan **konteksnya**. Kalau ada kata baru, mungkin itu **kata lokal**, bukan kesalahanmu: tanyakan *'Sorry, what does … mean?'*

blocks.text: **About the audio in this app:** every recording here is read by **one voice with one accent**. So in this lesson the recordings practise the **words and expressions** of each variety, never the accent itself. To hear real speakers from many countries, watch the video in the resources and listen for the features in this lesson.

id.text: **Tentang audio di aplikasi ini:** setiap rekaman di sini dibacakan oleh **satu suara dengan satu aksen**. Jadi di pelajaran ini rekamannya melatih **kata dan ungkapan** khas tiap ragam, bukan aksennya. Untuk mendengar penutur asli dari banyak negara, tonton video di bagian sumber dan dengarkan ciri-ciri dari pelajaran ini.

blocks.prompt: In a meeting, your colleague from Chennai uses a word you've never heard. What's the best first thought?
options: It's probably a mistake, so I'll ignore it.
It may be a local Indian English word, so I can politely ask what it means.
I should ask him to speak American English.
blocks.explain: Indian English has its own everyday words (like prepone or revert). A new word is often a local word, not a mistake. Asking 'Sorry, what does … mean?' is normal and professional.

id.prompt: Dalam rapat, rekanmu dari Chennai memakai kata yang belum pernah kamu dengar. Apa pikiran pertama yang paling tepat?
id.explain: Bahasa Inggris India punya kata sehari-hari sendiri (seperti prepone atau revert). Kata baru sering kali kata lokal, bukan kesalahan. Bertanya 'Sorry, what does … mean?' itu wajar dan profesional.
options: Mungkin salah, jadi saya abaikan saja.
Mungkin kata lokal bahasa Inggris India; saya bisa bertanya artinya dengan sopan.
Saya sebaiknya memintanya berbicara bahasa Inggris Amerika.

blocks.text: Before the accent, **words** tell you a lot. Here are common ones you'll meet at work and when you travel. You don't need to use them yourself: you need to **understand** them when you hear them.

id.text: Sebelum aksennya, **kata-katanya** sudah banyak memberi petunjuk. Ini kata-kata yang sering kamu temui di kantor dan saat bepergian. Kamu tidak perlu memakainya sendiri: yang penting kamu **mengerti** saat mendengarnya.

rows.en: The meeting room is on the first floor. Take the lift.
rows.id: Ruang rapatnya satu lantai di atas lantai dasar. Naik lift.
rows.note: UK. US: elevator. The UK first floor is the US second floor.

id.note: UK. US: elevator. First floor di Inggris = second floor di Amerika (lantai 2 kita).

rows.note: UK. US: on vacation.

id.note: UK. US: on vacation.

rows.note: Australia: arvo = afternoon. Also brekkie = breakfast.

id.note: Australia: arvo = afternoon (siang/sore). Juga brekkie = breakfast (sarapan).

rows.note: Australia (now common in the UK too): 'it's fine' or 'you're welcome'.

id.note: Australia (sekarang juga umum di Inggris): 'tidak apa-apa' atau 'sama-sama'.

rows.en: The meeting has been preponed to 9 a.m.
rows.note: India: prepone = move to an earlier time (the opposite of postpone).

id.note: India: prepone = memajukan jadwal (kebalikan dari postpone, menunda).

rows.id: Mohon dibalas paling lambat hari Jumat.
rows.note: India: revert = reply. In other varieties revert means 'go back to an earlier state'.

id.note: India: revert = membalas. Di ragam lain, revert berarti 'kembali ke keadaan sebelumnya'.

rows.note: India: do what is necessary.

id.note: India: lakukan apa yang perlu dilakukan.

rows.en: The budget is five lakh rupees.
rows.note: India: 1 lakh = 100,000; 1 crore = 10 million.

id.note: India: 1 lakh = 100.000; 1 crore = 10 juta.

rows.note: Singlish. The answer is 'Can' (yes) or 'Cannot' (no).

id.note: Singlish. Jawabannya 'Can' (bisa) atau 'Cannot' (tidak bisa).

rows.en: Don't worry lah, I settle it for you.
rows.id: Tenang saja, biar saya yang urus.
rows.note: Singlish: lah adds emphasis or reassurance; 'I settle' = I'll handle it.

id.note: Singlish: lah menambah penekanan atau menenangkan; 'I settle' = saya yang urus.

rows.note: Nigeria: I'm coming = I'll be right back (said when you leave for a moment).

id.note: Nigeria: I'm coming = saya segera kembali (diucapkan saat pergi sebentar).

rows.en: Sorry I'm late, there was a go-slow on the bridge.
rows.id: Maaf saya terlambat, tadi macet di jembatan.
rows.note: Nigeria: go-slow = traffic jam.

id.note: Nigeria: go-slow = kemacetan.

blocks.text: **Singlish particles** come at the end of a sentence and add feeling, a bit like Indonesian *dong*, *kok* or *-lah*: **lah** = emphasis or reassurance (*Don't worry lah*); **leh** = softer, a little persuading or unsure (*This one quite nice leh*); **lor** = 'that's how it is', accepting something (*No taxi, so take the MRT lor*). Their exact meaning depends on the tone, so understand them as feelings, not words to translate. In Standard Singapore English (reports, presentations, the news) you won't hear them.

id.text: **Partikel Singlish** muncul di akhir kalimat dan menambah rasa, mirip *dong*, *kok* atau *-lah* dalam bahasa Indonesia: **lah** = penekanan atau menenangkan (*Don't worry lah*); **leh** = lebih lembut, sedikit membujuk atau ragu (*This one quite nice leh*); **lor** = 'ya sudah, memang begitu', menerima keadaan (*No taxi, so take the MRT lor*). Arti persisnya tergantung nada, jadi pahami sebagai perasaan, bukan kata yang diterjemahkan. Di Standard Singapore English (laporan, presentasi, berita) partikel ini tidak dipakai.

blocks.text: **Indonesian traps.** Floors: in Indonesia (and the US) *lantai 1* is the level you enter from the street. In the UK that's the **ground floor**, and the **first floor** is one level up: a British receptionist's 'first floor' is your *lantai 2*. And Nigerian *I'm coming* doesn't mean the speaker is coming to you: it means 'wait, I'll be back soon'.

id.text: **Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia.** Lantai: di Indonesia (dan di Amerika) *lantai 1* adalah lantai yang kamu masuki dari jalan. Di Inggris itu disebut **ground floor**, dan **first floor** adalah satu lantai di atasnya: 'first floor' kata resepsionis di Inggris adalah *lantai 2* kita. Lalu, *I'm coming* versi Nigeria tidak berarti pembicara sedang datang ke tempatmu: artinya 'tunggu, saya segera kembali'.

blocks.prompt: Your colleague in Lagos says: 'Sorry, there was a terrible go-slow on the bridge.' What happened?
options: He was stuck in a traffic jam.
He walked slowly across the bridge.
The bridge was closed for repairs.
blocks.explain: In Nigerian English a go-slow is a traffic jam: the cars on the bridge were moving very slowly.

id.prompt: Rekanmu di Lagos berkata: 'Sorry, there was a terrible go-slow on the bridge.' Apa yang terjadi?
id.explain: Dalam bahasa Inggris Nigeria, go-slow adalah kemacetan: mobil-mobil di jembatan bergerak sangat pelan.

material.title: Sounds and rhythm: what to listen for

id.title: Bunyi dan irama: apa yang perlu didengarkan

blocks.text:
**1. r after a vowel** (a vowel = the sounds a, i, u, e, o) in words like *car*, *card*, *four*, *teacher*. It's one of the clearest clues.
- **Usually said:** the US and Canada, Ireland, Scotland, and much of India.
- **Usually not said** when no vowel follows: most of England, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and Nigeria. *car* = 'kaa', *teacher* = 'tee-chuh'.
- These speakers still say every r before a vowel (*red*, *very*), and often add it between words: *far away* → 'faa-raway'.
Indonesians always say the r, so your English has it, and that's fine too.

**2. Recap from B2:** in American English, t between vowels often sounds like a quick soft d (*water* → 'wader', *city* → 'ciddy'). In Australian English, the 'ay' in *day* or *mate* sounds close to 'ai', so *day* sounds like 'die' to outsiders.

**3. Rhythm.** British, American and Australian English are **stress-timed**: the stressed syllables (suku kata yang ditekan) come like a beat, and the weak syllables between them are squeezed into a short 'uh'. Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian English are often **syllable-timed**, like Indonesian: each syllable gets a similar length and a clearer vowel.

**4. Other features, as tendencies:**
- **India:** t and d are often said with the tip of the tongue curled back (**retroflex**), which sounds 'heavier'. Many speakers use one sound, between v and w, for both letters, so *very* and *west* may sound like 'wery' and 'vest'.
- **Singapore:** the last consonant of a word is often very soft or dropped (*stop* → 'sto', *act* → 'ak'), and long and short vowels can sound alike.
- **Nigeria:** weak syllables keep a full vowel (*about* → 'a-baut', *today* → 'tu-dei'), so speech can sound very clear and even.
- **In all three:** *th* often becomes t or d (*think* → 'tink', *this* → 'dis').

id.text:
**1. r setelah vokal** (vokal = bunyi a, i, u, e, o) di kata seperti *car*, *card*, *four*, *teacher*. Ini salah satu petunjuk paling jelas.
- **Biasanya dibaca:** Amerika dan Kanada, Irlandia, Skotlandia, dan sebagian besar India.
- **Biasanya tidak dibaca** kalau tidak ada vokal sesudahnya: sebagian besar Inggris, Australia, Selandia Baru, Singapura dan Nigeria. *car* = 'kaa', *teacher* = 'tii-cheu'.
- Penutur ini tetap membaca r sebelum vokal (*red*, *very*), dan sering menambahkannya di antara kata: *far away* → 'faa-raway'.
Orang Indonesia selalu membaca r, jadi bahasa Inggrismu punya r, dan itu juga tidak apa-apa.

**2. Ulangan dari B2:** dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika, t di antara dua vokal sering terdengar seperti d yang cepat dan lembut (*water* → 'wader', *city* → 'ciddy'). Dalam bahasa Inggris Australia, bunyi 'ei' di *day* atau *mate* mendekati 'ai', jadi *day* terdengar seperti 'die' bagi orang luar.

**3. Irama.** Bahasa Inggris Inggris, Amerika dan Australia **berirama tekanan** (stress-timed): suku kata yang ditekan datang seperti ketukan, dan suku kata lemah di antaranya dipendekkan jadi 'eu' yang singkat. Bahasa Inggris India, Singapura dan Nigeria sering **berirama suku kata** (syllable-timed), seperti bahasa Indonesia: tiap suku kata kira-kira sama panjang dan vokalnya lebih jelas.

**4. Ciri lain, sebagai kecenderungan:**
- **India:** t dan d sering diucapkan dengan ujung lidah melengkung ke belakang (**retroflex**), sehingga terdengar 'lebih berat'. Banyak penutur memakai satu bunyi, di antara v dan w, untuk kedua huruf itu, jadi *very* dan *west* bisa terdengar seperti 'wery' dan 'vest'.
- **Singapura:** konsonan terakhir sebuah kata sering sangat lemah atau hilang (*stop* → 'sto', *act* → 'ak'), dan vokal panjang dan pendek bisa terdengar sama.
- **Nigeria:** suku kata lemah tetap memakai vokal penuh (*about* → 'a-baut', *today* → 'tu-dei'), jadi ucapannya bisa terdengar sangat jelas dan rata.
- **Di ketiganya:** *th* sering jadi t atau d (*think* → 'tink', *this* → 'dis').

blocks.text: **Good news for Indonesians:** Indonesian is syllable-timed too, so the rhythm of Indian, Singaporean and Nigerian English often feels familiar. The harder rhythm for you is the British and American one, where weak syllables almost disappear. And don't judge a speaker by these features: a Nigerian engineer with full vowels or an Indian manager with a curled-back t is speaking their English correctly.

id.text: **Kabar baik untuk orang Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia juga berirama suku kata, jadi irama bahasa Inggris India, Singapura dan Nigeria sering terasa akrab. Irama yang lebih sulit bagimu justru irama Inggris dan Amerika, di mana suku kata lemah hampir hilang. Dan jangan menilai pembicara dari ciri-ciri ini: insinyur Nigeria dengan vokal penuh atau manajer India dengan t yang melengkung sedang berbicara dalam bahasa Inggrisnya dengan benar.

blocks.prompt: An American colleague talks about 'the wader bill' for the new office. What does she mean?
blocks.explain: In American English a t between two vowels often sounds like a quick, soft d, so water sounds like 'wader'. An office has a water bill (tagihan air).

id.prompt: Rekan dari Amerika membicarakan 'the wader bill' untuk kantor baru. Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: Dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika, t di antara dua vokal sering terdengar seperti d yang cepat dan lembut, jadi water terdengar seperti 'wader'. Kantor punya water bill (tagihan air).

blocks.text:
A **lingua franca** is a shared language between people whose first languages are different. When you talk to a supplier in Osaka, a partner NGO in Bangkok or a client in Berlin, none of you is a native speaker: that's **English as a lingua franca (ELF)**. Many, probably most, English conversations in the world are like this.

In ELF, **clear beats clever**:
- **Avoid idioms, slang and abbreviations:** *touch base*, *hit the ground running*, *ASAP*, *EOD*. Say *talk*, *start quickly*, *by Friday 5 p.m.*
- **One idea per sentence**, and slow down a little at the important parts.
- **Numbers, names, dates:** say key numbers digit by digit (*one-five*) and type them in the chat; spell names (*S for Surabaya*); write the month as a word (*3 April*), because *03/04* is 3 April in Indonesia and the UK but March 4 in the US.
- **Check with a summary**, not with *Do you understand?*: *Just to confirm, …* / *So, to sum up, …*
- **Paraphrase** when someone looks lost: *What I mean is …* / *Let me put it another way.*
- **Ask** when you don't understand: *Sorry, could you say that more slowly?*

id.text:
**Lingua franca** adalah bahasa bersama antara orang-orang yang bahasa pertamanya berbeda. Saat kamu berbicara dengan pemasok di Osaka, LSM mitra di Bangkok atau klien di Berlin, tidak ada yang penutur asli: itulah **bahasa Inggris sebagai lingua franca (ELF)**. Banyak, mungkin sebagian besar, percakapan bahasa Inggris di dunia seperti ini.

Dalam ELF, **jelas lebih penting daripada keren**:
- **Hindari idiom, slang dan singkatan:** *touch base*, *hit the ground running*, *ASAP*, *EOD*. Katakan *talk*, *start quickly*, *by Friday 5 p.m.*
- **Satu ide per kalimat**, dan sedikit perlambat di bagian penting.
- **Angka, nama, tanggal:** ucapkan angka penting digit per digit (*one-five*) dan ketik di chat; eja nama (*S for Surabaya*); tulis bulan dengan kata (*3 April*), karena *03/04* berarti 3 April di Indonesia dan Inggris tapi 4 Maret di Amerika.
- **Cek dengan ringkasan**, bukan dengan *Do you understand?*: *Just to confirm, …* / *So, to sum up, …*
- **Ucapkan ulang dengan kata lain** kalau lawan bicara tampak bingung: *What I mean is …* / *Let me put it another way.*
- **Bertanya** kalau kamu tidak mengerti: *Sorry, could you say that more slowly?*

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap: the polite yes.** In Indonesia (and in Japan, Thailand and many other places) it's polite to nod or say *yes* even when you didn't understand everything (sungkan). So *Do you understand?* almost always gets *Yes*. Ask for a summary instead (*Just to confirm, what are the next steps on your side?*) and give one yourself. And when YOU don't understand, say so: *Sorry, could you say that again more slowly?* is professional, not embarrassing.

id.text: **Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia: 'ya' karena sungkan.** Di Indonesia (dan di Jepang, Thailand dan banyak tempat lain) mengangguk atau bilang *yes* dianggap sopan walaupun belum mengerti semuanya. Jadi *Do you understand?* hampir selalu dijawab *Yes*. Lebih baik minta ringkasan (*Just to confirm, what are the next steps on your side?*) dan beri ringkasanmu sendiri. Dan kalau KAMU yang tidak mengerti, katakan saja: *Sorry, could you say that again more slowly?* itu profesional, bukan memalukan.

blocks.text: **The Lingua Franca Core.** The researcher Jennifer Jenkins studied which pronunciation features matter most when non-native speakers talk to each other. Most important: **clear consonants** (but *th* matters little: 'tink' for *think* is usually understood), keeping the sounds at the **start** of words (*street*, not 'set'), **long vs short vowels** (*ship* / *sheep*, *live* / *leave*: a trap for Indonesians, because Indonesian has no long vowels), and **stress on the key word** (*I said FIFTEEN, not fifty*). Much less important: a native-like accent, the exact vowel sound, weak forms like 'uh'. So don't spend your energy sounding British or American: spend it on being clear.

id.text: **Lingua Franca Core.** Peneliti Jennifer Jenkins meneliti ciri pelafalan mana yang paling penting saat penutur non-native berbicara satu sama lain. Paling penting: **konsonan yang jelas** (tapi *th* tidak terlalu penting: 'tink' untuk *think* biasanya tetap dimengerti), menjaga bunyi di **awal** kata (*street*, bukan 'set'), **vokal panjang vs pendek** (*ship* / *sheep*, *live* / *leave*: jebakan untuk orang Indonesia, karena bahasa Indonesia tidak punya vokal panjang), dan **tekanan pada kata kunci** (*I said FIFTEEN, not fifty*). Jauh kurang penting: aksen seperti penutur asli, bunyi vokal yang persis sama, bentuk lemah seperti 'eu'. Jadi jangan habiskan tenagamu untuk terdengar seperti orang Inggris atau Amerika: pakai untuk berbicara dengan jelas.

blocks.prompt: On a video call with partners from Germany and Korea, which sentence is the clearest?
options: Let's hit the ground running on Monday.
Let's kick things off EOD Monday.
Let's start the work on Monday morning.
blocks.explain: It says plainly what happens and when. 'Hit the ground running' and 'kick things off' are idioms, and 'EOD' (end of day) is an abbreviation: all of them can confuse partners who learnt English as an extra language.

id.prompt: Dalam video call dengan mitra dari Jerman dan Korea, kalimat mana yang paling jelas?
id.explain: Kalimat ini mengatakan dengan lugas apa yang terjadi dan kapan. 'Hit the ground running' dan 'kick things off' adalah idiom, dan 'EOD' (end of day, akhir hari kerja) adalah singkatan: semuanya bisa membingungkan mitra yang belajar bahasa Inggris sebagai bahasa tambahan.

id.intro: Selamat datang! Di kantor dan saat bepergian kamu akan bertemu penutur dari Inggris, Amerika dan Australia, tapi juga dari India, Singapura dan Nigeria, dan banyak orang yang, seperti kamu, berbahasa Inggris sebagai bahasa tambahan. Di pelajaran ini kamu belajar kata dan bunyi yang menandai tiap ragam, dan cara berbicara supaya jelas dimengerti saat bahasa Inggris menjadi bahasa bersama.

assessment.wng-1: Kamu sedang video call dengan Chidi, rekan kerja di Lagos, Nigeria. Ia berdiri dan mengatakan ini. Dengarkan. Apa maksudnya? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.wng-2: Wei Ling, rekan kerja di Singapura, mengirim pesan suara. Dengarkan. Apa yang ingin ia ketahui? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.wng-3: Mr Sharma, manajermu di Bengaluru, menutup email-nya dengan: 'The auditors arrive on Monday. Kindly do the needful.' Apa arti 'do the needful'? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.wng-4: Rina punya dua rekan kerja: Fiona dari Glasgow, Skotlandia, dan Mia dari Sydney, Australia. Keduanya mengucapkan kata 'car'. Siapa yang lebih mungkin membaca r-nya? Tulis namanya.
assessment.wng-5: Banyak penutur di Nigeria, India dan Singapura memberi setiap suku kata panjang yang mirip dan vokal yang jelas, seperti bahasa Indonesia. Bahasa Inggris Inggris dan Amerika justru memendekkan suku kata lemah di antara suku kata yang ditekan. Apa nama irama yang pertama? Tulis istilahnya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.wng-6: Jam 6 sore, rapat online yang panjang dengan mitra dari Thailand dan Jerman tidak ada kemajuan. Kamu ingin bilang 'Let's call it a day.' Katakan dengan kata-kata sederhana, tanpa idiom itu. Tulis satu kalimat pendek dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.wng-7: Di sambungan telepon yang buruk, Somchai, pemasok di Bangkok, menyebutkan harga per kotak. Kamu tidak yakin ia bilang 'fifteen' atau 'fifty'. Tulis satu pertanyaan pendek dalam bahasa Inggris untuk mengecek angkanya.
